source: SEP (Bartha) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, on Hesse 1966
finding: Hesse's material criteria: (1) material analogy, horizontal similarities must include observable similarities; (2) causal condition, vertical relations in the source must be causal in an acceptable scientific sense; (3) no essential difference, essential source properties and causal relations must not sit in the negative analogy.
numbers: Three conditions. Franklin 1749 listed 12 shared properties of electricity and lightning; the 13th (attraction to points) had no known causal link to them. Fluid-flow analogy of heat failed once heat was found not conserved.
limits: Criticised as too narrow (mathematics has no material analogy), causal condition too strict, essentiality test ignores inferential context (rectangle-box case). Secondary source for Hesse.
agent_relevance: Conditions 2 and 3 are the testable ones: a code check can ask for a stated causal link in the source and scan listed differences for items tied to that link.

source: SEP on Bartha's articulation model
finding: Bartha starts from vertical relations in the source, not overall similarity. A good analogical argument needs (a) prior association: a clear connection in the source between the positive analogy and the hypothetical analogy, and (b) potential for generalization: no known critical disanalogy.
numbers: Worked case: square maximises area for fixed perimeter; cube maximises volume for fixed surface area. Method: state the source proof precisely, list the concepts it uses, check each has a target analogue. Plausibility is prima facie (worth investigating), not a probability.
limits: Needs a source argument precise enough to inspect; weak where the source has no proof or mechanism (e.g. animal-drug testing).
agent_relevance: Best fit for a code guardrail: a record with the source connection and a list of critical features, each marked has-analogue yes/no/unknown. Output is 'worth testing', never a probability.

source: SEP on Bartha's justification and simplified criteria
finding: Justification rests on van Fraassen's symmetry principle: problems that are essentially the same get essentially the same solution. Modal form: if problems might be essentially the same, they might have the same solution. Simplified test: non-trivial positive analogy plus no known critical disanalogy.
numbers: No numbers. Claim is qualitative.
limits: Modal, so it yields only 'prima facie plausible'. Critics note it gives no graded strength.
agent_relevance: Fits a gate that outputs candidate or not-candidate, matching G3: a candidate still needs a held-out check.
quote: problems which are essentially the same must receive essentially the same solution

source: SEP on common-sense guidelines G1-G8 for analogical arguments
finding: Eight textbook guidelines: more similarities strengthen; more differences weaken; more ignorance weakens; weaker conclusion more plausible; causal analogies beat non-causal; structural beat superficial; relevance of similarities and differences must be weighed; multiple analogies strengthen.
numbers: The SEP shows they pull in different directions. Reid's life-on-planets argument: Stebbing rates it suggestive because the conclusion is weak (G4); Mill rejects it because of vast ignorance (G3).
limits: Counting similarities is ill-defined; G7 (relevance) carries all the weight and is not operational.
agent_relevance: Counting rules should not be coded as a strength score. Only the relevance-to-conclusion link is worth checking.

source: SEP on structure-mapping systematicity vs causal relevance (McKay 1993; Lee and Holyoak 2008)
finding: Systematicity can mislead. Microbes in Antarctic frozen lakes support life on Mars. Freezing is a preventive cause. Present Mars is more systematically like Antarctica than ancient Mars is, but ancient Mars was warmer and more life-friendly. So higher systematicity gave a worse inference.
numbers: Qualitative example. SEP cites Lee and Holyoak 2008 for the point that systematicity does not always raise plausibility and that causal direction (generative vs preventive) matters.
limits: Argues from cases, not data. The primary Lee and Holyoak experiment was NOT opened this session (search budget gone).
agent_relevance: A purely structural overlap score is not a valid analogical-argument check. The check must know whether a shared factor helps or blocks the effect.
quote: There is no short-cut via syntax.

source: SEP on Norton's material theory of analogy
finding: Norton rejects any universal rule. Each analogical inference is warranted by a local fact, a low-level uniformity shared by source and target.
numbers: Example: Galileo's lunar mountains; light points ahead of the sunlight edge on the moon, as on Earth mountains. No numerical values given.
limits: Works poorly when the uniformity is itself the target (rectangle-box, life on other planets).
agent_relevance: Rival to Hesse and Bartha. Argues a generic code guardrail is not sufficient; it should make the model name the local uniformity and then test it.
quote: these embellished schema never seem to be quite embellished enough

source: SEP on Davies-Russell determination rules and Weitzenfeld
finding: If background knowledge says Q is determined by P1..Pm, and source and target agree on every Pi, then Q transfers deductively. Weitzenfeld treats the rule as a missing enthymematic premise.
numbers: Used-car example: value fixed by six factors (year, make, mileage, condition, colour, accident history). Cars identical on all six have the same value.
limits: Rule is rarely known; for animal drug testing, establishing it is as hard as the original question.
agent_relevance: The only variant that is fully code-checkable: store the determination rule as a list of factors and compare source and target on each. Falls back to Bartha when the rule is unknown.

source: SEP on Dardashti et al. analogue confirmation (Hawking radiation)
finding: Observations on lab analogues (dumb holes) are claimed to confirm predictions about black holes, given an exact formal analogy and extra assumptions. This is new evidence from the analogue, not just the old analogy.
numbers: No numbers. SEP calls the claim controversial.
limits: Needs a formal analogy and a universality argument; contested.
agent_relevance: Shows a route from analogy to evidence: run the analogue, then check the prediction. Matches G3 (test on something not fitted).

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models: digit matrices
finding: Zero-shot GPT-3 beat UCLA undergraduates on text digit matrices, but some people beat it.
numbers: Human N=40. Generative: GPT-3 vs human odds ratio 1.88 (p=0.005). Multiple choice: OR 6.27 (p=2.3e-8). Pattern across problem types correlated with humans, r(30)=0.39.
limits: Possible training contamination; text task is new but rule structure is Raven-like. See Lewis and Mitchell for variants.
agent_relevance: Headline success on a novel format; later robustness work cuts it down.

source: Webb et al. (2023) story analogies: causal-structure sensitivity
finding: Materials from Gentner et al.: pick the target story that shares the source's causal relations when first-order relations are matched. GPT-3 was above chance in near analogy but not far analogy; students clearly beat GPT-3.
numbers: Humans N=54. Combined: GPT-3 binomial p=0.0005, humans t(53)=21.3. Near analogy: GPT-3 p=0.0039. Far analogy: GPT-3 p=0.065 (ns), humans t(53)=16.7. GPT-3 vs human OR 0.37 (p=0.0003). 15 of 54 students were perfect. Initial GPT-4 check was better in far analogy.
limits: GPT-3 only; GPT-4 reported as preliminary. This is the nearest test of whether the model sees the causal link.
agent_relevance: Without a causal-link check, a bare model is weak exactly where Hesse's criterion matters: cross-domain causal mapping.

source: Webb et al. (2023) verbal analogies with causal relation types
finding: On the Jones et al. set (categorical, compositional, causal relations), GPT-3 was in the human range but numerically weaker. GPT-3 also showed the human cost of semantically distant analogs.
numbers: On UCLA VAT and Sternberg-Nigro sets GPT-3 matched or beat MTurk adults; on SAT analogies it beat the estimated high-school average.
limits: Exact per-relation numbers not extracted from the figures.
agent_relevance: Causal relation items were the weaker class, consistent with the story-task result.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs: letter strings
finding: Replication with counterfactual variants (permuted alphabets, symbol alphabets). Humans stayed high on simple problems; GPT models fell sharply. With one to three generalisations, both humans and models did poorly on original and variants.
numbers: Prolific humans N=263 (4 excluded), 14 problems each. Human mean beat every GPT model in all cells, by a wide margin at zero generalisations. Error analysis: alternative rule used in 38.59 percent of human errors, 22.00 percent of GPT-4 errors, 5.81 percent of GPT-3 errors.
limits: Per-cell accuracies were garbled in the text extraction; headline direction is certain.
agent_relevance: Success on the standard form can be memory of the form. Any analogy gate must be tested on a mutated version of the problem (G3).
quote: exhibiting brittleness on most of the variations we tested

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) digit matrices variants
finding: Moving the blank position at random: humans unchanged, GPT models dropped dramatically. Replacing digits with symbols: both unchanged.
numbers: Prolific humans N=301 (1 rejected), 10 matrix problems each.
limits: Only one of two variants broke the models, so the failure is specific, not general.
agent_relevance: Position of the answer slot is a surface cue the model leaned on; vary format when verifying.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) story analogies: order and paraphrase
finding: Far-analogy story task (18 problems) is biased by answer order for GPT-4 but not for humans, and paraphrasing the correct target lowers GPT-4 more than humans.
numbers: Webb's GPT-4 data: 89 percent (16/18) when the right answer is first, 61 percent (11/18) when second. Lewis-Mitchell GPT-4: first 100, second 72, total 86 percent (31/36) as read from Table 4. Humans N=245: 78 percent either order (564/720). Paraphrase: GPT-4 86 to 72 percent (26/36); humans 78 to 70 percent (503/720).
limits: Sentence-level similarity of the correct target to the source was a shortcut for both. GPT-4 0613 only. Table columns were garbled; row assignment inferred.
agent_relevance: Randomise option order and paraphrase before trusting a model's pick between two analogies.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) counterfactual tasks, CogSci version
finding: Short first report of the letter-string counterfactuals: GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 do worse on nonstandard alphabets while humans stay high.
numbers: Numbers in the 2411.14215 lines. Models fall short on counterfactuals even when comprehension checks of the alphabet pass.
limits: Same models and data family as the longer paper; not independent.
agent_relevance: Supports the approximate-retrieval reading rather than rule-based transfer.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives, zero-shot
finding: Models separate near analogies from distractors but fail on far analogies. GPT-4 scored below chance on far analogies.
numbers: 548 pairs; 120 items (10 percent) checked by two human assistants. Overall: humans 96.0, models 57.3 (chance 50). Near analogy: humans 97.9, models 75.0. Far analogy: humans 94.1, models 39.6. By partition: near analogy vs far distractor 76.9; near vs near 73.2; far vs far 45.3; far analogy vs near distractor 33.9.
limits: Binary task; narratives built from proverbs; SBERT similarity alone reached 77.9 percent on near analogies.
agent_relevance: Models follow surface similarity over relational system match when the two conflict, the failure Bartha's test must block.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: what helps
finding: Solved examples and chain-of-thought improved results, but even in the few-shot setting the best model got only halfway between chance and humans. Action overlap was the most distracting surface element.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot mean 68.1 percent, SBERT 42.3 percent; human 96.0. Exact few-shot gains not extracted.
limits: Prompt instructions asking for system mappings did not fix the 33.9 percent case.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to use relational structure is not enough; use code-held checks.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Prompt the model to recall relevant solved problems and knowledge before solving. Beats 0-shot CoT and few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench; average gain about 4 percent.
numbers: Models: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, PaLM2, text-davinci-003. K=5 self-generated exemplars on GSM8K, K=3 on MATH and BIG-Bench; Codeforces adds self-generated knowledge. Gain over few-shot CoT largest on MATH. Table cells garbled, so only the paper-stated average is recorded.
limits: Fails with weak models: with curie-001 and davinci-001, retrieved labelled exemplars beat self-generation. More output tokens. Sensitive to prompt wording.
agent_relevance: Analogy as a retrieval prompt helps only if the model is strong and the exemplar relevant. It does not verify the analogy.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) exemplar relevance and scale
finding: Self-generated exemplars help because they are tailored to the problem; fixed exemplars from a nearby topic may not match. Self-generation beats retrieved exemplars only from text-davinci-002 upward.
numbers: Scale ablation on GSM8K across four base models from text-curie-001 to text-davinci-003.
limits: Relevance shown by qualitative examples, not a relevance metric.
agent_relevance: Relevance of the source decides benefit; a check that exemplar and target share the critical feature would apply Bartha's prior association.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: New tasks mapping between words and abstract symbols. Advanced LLMs match humans in several conditions but respond differently to some variations and to semantic distractors.
numbers: Compared humans, GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Llama-405B and others. In the Defaults condition GPT-4 was not significantly different from humans; GPT-4 dropped 0.6 and 0.4 in two random-final conditions relative to Defaults (read from text).
limits: Some numbers read from garbled text; direction solid.
agent_relevance: Matching human accuracy does not show humanlike mechanism; keep a code check rather than trusting the model's own account.
quote: LLMs might offer a how-possibly explanation

source: Opielka, Rosenbusch, Stevenson (2025) Analogical reasoning inside LLMs: concept vectors
finding: Verbal concepts (antonym, category) have invariant internal representations; abstract concepts (previous, next) do not. A correct internal concept can coexist with a wrong output.
numbers: Llama-3.1 70B: 98 percent on previous/next items but 62 percent on abstract previous/next tasks. Zero-shot, function vectors beat concept vectors (50 vs 14 percent for 8B; 58 vs 2 percent for 70B). Top-100 heads overlap 89 percent across metrics.
limits: Open-weights models only; correlational plus steering evidence.
agent_relevance: The model may hold the relation internally yet fail to apply it, so a code-side check of the relation is a separate safeguard.

source: Hu, Storks, Lewis, Chai (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Zero-shot PLMs on Raven's matrices converted to language performed above human level and near supervised vision methods; higher-level abstraction in the encoding improved results.
numbers: Abstract page only: no numbers stated.
limits: Abstract only; numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Webb: strong on structured forms, so robustness variants (Lewis and Mitchell) are the right test.

source: Wijesiriwardene et al. (2023) ANALOGICAL long-text analogy benchmark
finding: Benchmark with six complexity levels, 13 datasets, three distance measures, 8 LLMs. It gets harder to identify analogies higher up the taxonomy.
numbers: Abstract page only: no scores stated.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A complexity ladder suggests starting an analogy gate on simple causal cases only.
quote: increasingly challenging for LLMs to identify analogies when going up the analogy taxonomy

source: SEP on what is NOT established: Bayesian and inductive-logic treatments
finding: No accepted formal logic of analogical strength: Carnapian rules, Bayesian conditionalisation and liberal Bayesianism each leave a 'dark corner' of unconstrained revision. Argumentation theorists dispute whether analogical arguments are deductive.
numbers: No numbers. Govier 1999, Waller 2001, Guarini 2004, Kraus 2015 hold differing views on deductive status.
limits: This is why Hesse and Bartha stay as criteria, not as a probability.
agent_relevance: Do not output a calibrated probability for an analogical claim; output the status of each criterion.

source: SEP on Aristotle's criteria for analogical arguments (Hesse's ancestor)
finding: Aristotle already gave four criteria: strength grows with number of similarities; similarity reduces to shared properties and relations; good analogies come from common causes or general laws; a good analogical argument need not presuppose the general rule.
numbers: No numbers. Example: sea salt explained by analogy with sweat as a residue of growth (Meteorologica 358a17).
limits: Secondary source; criteria 1 and 3 pull apart, as with later counting versus causal views.
agent_relevance: The causal-link criterion is old and stable across 2300 years; the counting criterion is the weak one.
